title: My day
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: One Latin present does the work of two English ones. Legō is 'I read' and 'I am reading', and there is no progressive to build — no 'am', no '-ing', nothing to choose between. Whenever English offers you two tenses here, Latin offers one.

The ending is the subject, and this is the module where you can see it move: legō 'I read', legis 'you read', legit 'he reads'. Three people, one word each time, and the pronoun is left out unless you want to press on who — which M2 already said about tū.

Verbs come in families and the endings differ between them. legō drops to legis, but labōrō keeps its a — labōrat — and veniō keeps its i. The -ō of 'I' is shared; everything in front of it has to be learned per verb, which is why a dictionary gives you two shapes and not one.

Motion takes ad plus the object shape: ad scholam eō. This is the first preposition in the course, and the noun after it wears the same -m it wears as an object — the preposition does not excuse it from having an ending.

Time words like cotīdiē, semper and saepe never change shape and sit wherever they are needed, usually in front. They are adverbs, and an adverb in Latin has nobody to agree with — so these are the cheapest words in the module.

eō is 'I go', and it is also a shape of other words entirely — you will meet it later as 'by that' and as 'to there'. Here it is the verb, nothing else, and its shapes are eō, īs, it and the infinitive īre. Watch the tiny ones: it is a whole sentence meaning 'he goes'.

venit means 'he comes'. Hold that spelling: in the next module you will meet vēnit with a bar, which is 'he came'. One mark is the entire difference between the two tenses, and a Roman hears the length as clearly as you hear the difference between 'ship' and 'sheep'.

words.note: 'To, towards', and the noun after it takes the object shape — ad scholam, never ad schola. The first preposition in the course, and it never changes.
'School' — schola as the subject, scholam after ad. In Latin it meant the teaching rather than the building, so 'I go to school' is closer to 'I go to lessons'.
'I go': eō, īs 'you go', it 'he/she goes', īre 'to go'. Tiny and irregular — it is a complete sentence on its own.

sentences.trap: schola became scholam after ad. English prepositions leave their noun alone, so nothing warns you that a word can need an ending because of what stands in front of it.
sentences.sound: AD SCHO-lam E-ō. The ch is a hard k with a breath after it, not the ch of 'church'. eō is two syllables — E-o — and the ō is long.

words.note: 'Every day' in one word, and it never changes. It usually comes first, which is where English would put 'every day' only for emphasis.

mistake.why: A progressive assembled out of 'to be' and a verbal noun, the way English builds 'am going'. Latin has no such construction in the present at all: eō alone is both 'I go' and 'I am going'.

sentences.usage: The ordinary way to describe a routine.

words.note: 'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one. The e drops out as soon as an ending is added.
'I read' AND 'I am reading' — one present for both: legō, legis 'you read', legit 'he reads', legere 'to read'. The e shortens to i before the endings.

sentences.trap: The cue says 'I am reading' and the Latin has one word for it. There is nothing here to match 'am' and nothing to match '-ing', and hunting for them is hunting for a construction Latin does not have.
sentences.sound: LI-brum LE-gō. Hard g. The ō is long and says 'I'.

mistake.why: 'I am reading' built out of two pieces because English needs two. Latin's present already covers it, and this construction says something much stranger — roughly 'I am a reading thing'.

sentences.trap: Two words, and one of them is the whole verb with its subject inside it. This is the shape to aim for: a Latin sentence can be shorter than the English one it translates without leaving anything out.

mistake.why: The pronoun put in out of habit. It is not wrong Latin, but ego means 'I, as against other people', and a sentence about your own routine rarely wants that contrast — M2 made the same point about tū.

sentences.mnemonic: 'Semper' is the 'always' English borrowed and kept.

words.note: 'Letter' — the written kind. epistula as the subject, epistulam as the object. English kept it in 'epistle'.
'I write': scrībō, scrībit 'he writes', scrībere 'to write'. The ī is long and stays long — which is what the English 'scribe' and 'describe' keep.

sentences.trap: epistulam looks plural because of the -am, and is not. It is one letter in its object shape — the same -am aqua takes, on a noun of the same family.
sentences.sound: e-PIS-tu-lam SCRI-bō. Both long vowels are stressed: the i of epistulam is short, so the stress falls back onto -pis-.

sentences.usage: Said about correspondence, then and now.

'I work' — ordinary work, not toil: labōrō, labōrat 'he works'. It keeps its a before the ending, where legō changes to legis.

sentences.trap: labōrō is not 'I labour'. English kept the word and narrowed it to hard or unpleasant work; the Latin covers any work at all, including a scholar's.
sentences.sound: co-TI-di-ē la-BO-rō. Both of labōrō's o-sounds are long, and the stress sits on the first of them.

variations.changed: a third person, and the a is still there

mistake.why: The third person built on legō's pattern. labōrō belongs to a different family and keeps its a: labōrat. There is no way to guess which family a verb is in — it comes with the word.

sentences.mnemonic: labōrō is any work; 'laborious' is English's narrowing of it.

words.note: 'Often', and it never changes. The ae is one sound, said like the 'eye' in English — SIGH-pe.
'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā as the thing needed. Three shapes of one word.
'To drink', the infinitive bibere — the shape a dictionary lists second. bibō 'I drink', bibis 'you drink', bibit 'he/she drinks'.

sentences.trap: The ae of saepe is not two vowels read in turn. It is one sound, and it is the 'eye' of English — a learner who says 'SAY-pe' has said a syllable Latin does not have.
sentences.sound: SIGH-pe A-quam BI-bō. The ae is the diphthong of 'eye'; the ō of bibō is long.

mistake.why: The object shape dropped again. The pattern is worth naming: every verb in this module that takes a thing puts that thing in the -m shape, and the time word in front changes nothing about it.

sentences.usage: Said about a habit, at any scale.

words.note: 'To, towards', and the noun after it takes the object shape — ad scholam, never ad schola. The first preposition in the course, and it never changes.

'He goes' — two letters, and a whole sentence. It is not the English 'it': Latin has no such word here, and the person is carried by the -t.

sentences.trap: it is not English 'it'. It is 'he goes' or 'she goes', and the two letters happening to spell an English word is the sharpest false friend in the course so far.

words.note: A Roman woman's given name, said YOO-li-a. Spelled with an i because Latin has no letter j at all.

'She comes': veniō 'I come', venit 'he/she comes', venīre 'to come'. Learn this spelling exactly — vēnit, with a bar, is 'she CAME', and M5 teaches it.

sentences.trap: This is the present, and the next module's vēnit is the past. The only difference on the page is the bar over the e, so the two tenses of this verb are one mark apart — and the mark is the tense.
sentences.sound: YOO-li-a co-TI-di-ē VE-nit. Every vowel in venit is SHORT. Clip them: VEN-it, quickly, and hear how different it will be from VAY-nit next time.

words.note: 'I read' AND 'I am reading' — one present for both: legō, legis 'you read', legit 'he reads', legere 'to read'. The -re ending is what makes it 'to'.
'I want' — irregular, and the only verb for wanting: volō 'I want', vult 'he/she wants'. It takes an object or an infinitive, and both come before it.

sentences.trap: The infinitive comes first, as it did in M3. English says 'I want to read' and Latin says 'to-read I-want' — and that order holds however long the sentence gets.
sentences.sound: LE-ge-re VO-lō. Three light syllables then two, with the stress on the first of each word.
